blocks.title: Vectors
blocks.text: Vectors are those physical quantities which have magnitude as well as direction for their complete specification.

blocks.caption: Examples of vectors
rows: the change in position of an object: a distance (magnitude) and a direction
the speed of an object in a particular direction
the rate of change of velocity, in either speed or direction or both
a push or pull acting on an object, determined by its magnitude and direction

blocks.text: A good way to represent a vector quantity is a vector diagram, in which vectors are represented by arrows: the length of the arrow indicates the magnitude and the head of the arrow shows the direction of the vector. Vectors are typically denoted by bold-face letters (V, F) or by an arrow head above the symbol.

A component of a vector is its effective value in a given direction. A vector may be considered as the resultant of its component vectors along specified directions, and it is usually convenient to resolve a vector into its components along mutually perpendicular directions; such components are called rectangular components. Let a vector A be represented by a line OP making an angle theta with the x-axis. Draw the projection OM of A on the x-axis and the projection ON on the y-axis (Fig. 2.1). The projection OM along the x-direction is represented by Ax and the projection ON along the y-direction by Ay. By the head-to-tail rule, A = Ax + Ay ... (2.1). Thus Ax and Ay are the components of A, and since they are at right angles to each other they are the rectangular components of A. Considering the right-angled triangle OMP, the magnitude of Ax, the x-component, is Ax = A cos theta ... (2.2), and the magnitude of Ay, the y-component, is Ay = A sin theta ... (2.3).

blocks.alt: Top left: vector A from O to P at angle theta with components Ax to M and Ay to N and the component formulae. Top middle: A and B from a common origin with the projection B cos theta on A and the dot-product formulae. Top right: A and B in a plane with A x B pointing out of it by the right-hand rule. blocks.caption: Vectors: rectangular components, scalar product and vector product (original diagram after Figures 2.1 to 2.4 and topics 2.1 to 2.3).
blocks.long_description: A vector drawn from the origin at an angle to the x-axis is the sum of two perpendicular components, one along x equal to the magnitude times the cosine of the angle and one along y equal to the magnitude times the sine, and the magnitude and direction are recovered from the components by Pythagoras and the tangent. The scalar product of two vectors is the product of their magnitudes and the cosine of the angle between them, equal to one magnitude times the projection of the other on it, so it is commutative, zero for perpendicular vectors, the product of magnitudes for parallel ones and the square of the magnitude for a vector with itself; work done is the scalar product of force and displacement. The vector product has magnitude equal to the product of the magnitudes and the sine of the angle, is directed perpendicular to the plane of the two vectors by the right-hand rule, reverses sign when the order is reversed, is zero for parallel vectors, equals the area of the parallelogram they span, and gives torque and the magnetic force on a moving charge.

blocks.text: Determination of a vector from its rectangular components

If the rectangular components of a vector (Fig. 2.1) are given, the magnitude of the vector follows from the Pythagorean theorem. In the right-angled triangle OMP, (OP)^2 = (OM)^2 + (MP)^2, or A^2 = Ax^2 + Ay^2 ... (2.4), or A = sqrt(Ax^2 + Ay^2). The direction theta is given by tan theta = MP/OM = Ay/Ax, or theta = tan^-1 (Ay/Ax) ... (2.5).

blocks.title: Example 2.1
blocks.text: Find the angle between two forces of equal magnitude when the magnitude of their resultant is also equal to the magnitude of either force. Solution: let theta be the angle between F1 and F2, with F1 along the x-axis. The x-component of the resultant is Rx = F1 cos 0 + F2 cos theta = F1 + F2 cos theta, and the y-component is Ry = F1 sin 0 + F2 sin theta = F2 sin theta. The resultant R is given by R^2 = Rx^2 + Ry^2. As R = F1 = F2 = F, F^2 = (F + F cos theta)^2 + (F sin theta)^2 = F^2 + F^2 cos^2 theta + 2 F^2 cos theta + F^2 sin^2 theta, or 0 = 2 F^2 cos theta + F^2 (cos^2 theta + sin^2 theta) = 2 F^2 cos theta + F^2, so cos theta = -0.5 and theta = cos^-1 (-0.5) = 120 degrees.

blocks.caption: Components of a vector
rows: Ax = A cos theta, Ay = A sin theta

blocks.prompt: A force of 20 N acts at 60 degrees above the horizontal. Find its rectangular components, and then recover its magnitude and direction from them.
blocks.explanation: Fx = 20 cos 60 = 10 N and Fy = 20 sin 60 = 17.3 N. Back again: F = sqrt(10^2 + 17.3^2) = sqrt(100 + 300) = 20 N, and theta = tan^-1 (17.3/10) = tan^-1 (1.73) = 60 degrees.

items: Vector: magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, acceleration, force); drawn as an arrow, written in bold or with an arrow over the symbol.
Rectangular components: A = Ax + Ay, Ax = A cos theta, Ay = A sin theta; back: A = sqrt(Ax^2 + Ay^2), theta = tan^-1 (Ay/Ax). Example 2.1: equal forces with an equal resultant are 120 degrees apart.
